subject: Archaeology
title: Sieving and Flotation: Finding the Tiny Stuff
description: Learn Sieving and Flotation: Finding the Tiny Stuff in one minute.

hook.text: The most important finds on a dig often fit on a fingertip — seeds, fish bones, and insect wings tell huge stories.

buildup.text: Soil from excavations is pushed through mesh sieves. Anything larger than the mesh holes is collected and sorted.

discovery.text: Flotation works differently: soil is stirred in water. Light organic material — seeds, charcoal — floats to the surface.

twist.text: A single charred seed can reveal what ancient people ate, what crops they grew, and what climate they lived in.

climax.text: Flotation at Çatalhöyük revealed the earliest known domesticated wheat — evidence that farming began in Turkey.

punchline.text: A seed smaller than a pea proved where farming began.

quiz.question: How does flotation help archaeologists?
options: It dissolves soil to expose buried structures
Light organic material like seeds and charcoal floats to the surface for collection
It measures the water content of soil to determine the age of deposits

details.summary: Sieving and flotation recover tiny artifacts and biological remains that excavators cannot see in the soil. Dry and wet sieving catches small bones, beads, and tool fragments. Flotation uses water to separate carbonized seeds, fish bones, and insect remains from soil, revealing diet and environment.
details.whyItMatters: The smallest finds often carry the most information. A carbonized seed reveals what people ate. A tiny bead indicates trade connections. Without sieving and flotation, this evidence — invisible during excavation — would be lost forever.
takeaways: Sieving catches small artifacts invisible during excavation
Flotation separates carbonized plant remains from soil using water
These methods recover critical evidence about diet and environment

faq.question: How does flotation work?
faq.answer: Soil is poured into a tank of water. Carbonized plant material — seeds, chaff, charcoal — floats to the surface and is caught in a fine mesh. Heavier items like bone and stone sink to a bottom sieve. The floating material, called the light fraction, is dried and sorted under microscopes.

faq.question: Why is flotation important for understanding ancient diets?
faq.answer: Carbonized seeds survive when accidentally charred during food processing. Flotation recovers these seeds in quantities that reveal crop types, wild foods gathered, and agricultural practices.
